title: Choosing between things
intro: Every time you choose, you give something up. Seeing that helps you pick what matters most to you.
explanation: Money can only be spent once. If you choose one thing, you give up what else that money could have done. That's a tradeoff.
Some things are needs: things you must have, like getting home or lunch on a school trip. Others are wants: nice to have, but you could manage without. Cover needs first, then wants.
A choice that repeats adds up. Spending {m:200} a week instead of saving it comes to {m:800} over 4 weeks.
There's no single right answer. A good choice is one that fits what you care about.

example.title: The game or the day out
lines: A game costs {m:1200}. A day out costs {m:800}.
Both together cost {m:2000}, which is more than Jo has.
Picking the game means giving up the day out, for now.
Picking the day out leaves {m:700}, which isn't enough for the game.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a need?

options.text: A game you'd like to try
options.feedback: Not quite. A game is fun, but you could manage without it. That makes it a want.

options.text: A coat, as yours no longer fits
options.feedback: Yes. You need a coat that fits.
Not quite. Stickers are a nice extra. That makes them a want.

hints: A need is something you must have.
Which one would leave you stuck if you didn't have it?
practice.correct: Right. A coat that fits is a need. The others are nice extras.
